precepts.text: Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?
precepts.point: Faithful are the wounds of a friend, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
precepts.why:
“Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.” The last part is the point: the kisses of an enemy are deceitful. And Luke shows the kiss: “Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?” Judas betrayed Christ with a kiss. The man betrayed him with the very sign of love.

Today we do not greet each other with a kiss like that, but we have our own greeting: Shalom, Captain, Most High bless. That is the betrayal. The embrace, the salute, the Shalom, and then the knife. That is the kiss of an enemy.

We saw it in 2018. A man who had been in another man’s house, greeting him with Shalom, barbecuing together, traveling together, came to that same man’s house, took all his furniture and put his children on the cold floor to sleep. He did not care. Not only did he betray the man, he betrayed all his children.

There is nothing worse than a traitor. And some of you think once you betray your brother or your sister, that is the end of it. It is not. The one who betrays with a kiss will be dealt with too. That is why the kisses of an enemy are called deceitful: Judas is the pattern of the familiar hand that destroys.

precepts.text: You do not know what shall be tomorrow, for life is a vapor; you ought to say, if the Most High wills, we shall do this or that.
precepts.point: Let another man praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips. Do not be boastful.
precepts.why:
“Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth.” James says the same: “Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain: Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.”

You do not know what will be tomorrow, for your life is a vapor. So James says what you ought to say instead: “For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.” If the Most High wills, we will do this or that.

None of us knows how much time we have; the Most High draws the line. Moses spoke unadvisedly at the waters of strife and was told he would not enter the promised land, and though he died in full strength at 120, the Most High set the end of his days. That is why you do not boast of tomorrow, and why you let another man praise you and not your own mouth.

precepts.point: Faithful are the wounds of a friend, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
precepts.why:
“Open rebuke is better than secret love.” Many of us leaving the Christian church were shocked to see men stood up and rebuked openly, but that is the law, and the law does it so that people may learn to fear the Most High.

Achan in Joshua 7 is the pattern. His sin was found out before all Israel, and he, with his family and his substance, was stoned and burned before all. Nothing about it was done in secret; the whole camp saw the rebuke and the judgment, so the whole camp learned to fear.

That open rebuke is a faithful wound from a friend. Secret love that lets a man go on in his sin is the kiss of an enemy, and the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.

precepts.text: The sleep of a laboring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much.
precepts.point: He that blesses his friend with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him. You may have worked fourteen or sixteen hours and are trying to get the last few winks before punching the clock, and a friend calling, texting, or banging on the door early breaks that sweet sleep. Ecclesiastes says the sleep of a laboring man is sweet.
precepts.why:
“He that blesseth his friend with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him.” You may have worked fourteen or sixteen hours and are trying to get the last few winks before punching the clock, and a friend calling, texting, or banging on the door early breaks that sweet sleep. His blessing is a curse to you.

Solomon says what that sleep is worth: “The sleep of a labouring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep.” The laboring man's sleep is sweet whether he ate little or much, and the friend with the loud voice at daybreak is taking it from him.

precepts.text: A covetous man's eye is never satisfied with his portion.
precepts.point: As the fining pot for silver and the furnace for gold, so is a man to his praise. Though you bray a fool in a mortar with a pestle, his foolishness will not depart from him.
precepts.why:
“Hell and destruction are never full; so the eyes of man are never satisfied.” Eyes that are never satisfied go into covetousness.

Ecclesiasticus says it plainly: “A covetous man’s eye is not satisfied with his portion; and the iniquity of the wicked drieth up his soul.” The covetous man's eye is never satisfied with his portion, and that iniquity dries up his soul. Like hell and destruction, it never gets full.

We are meant to be satisfied with our own portion. The eye that is never satisfied is the covetous eye, and it is the wicked whose soul it dries up.
